```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

```

```{r setup}
library(allocatR)
library(httptest)
```

This vignette covers use of the allocatR package to randomly assign participants
in a randomised clinical trial. It assumes that R can be connected to your trial
infrastructure through one of the following:

* R is run directly on the server containing trial data
* R is run remotely using an API call to the server containing trial data
* Randomisation is fully self-contained within e.g. a locally run Shiny app for managing randomisation.

The specific method of integration is beyond the scope of this vignette and will
vary with your implementation. This vignette assumes that randomisation code is
being run on a server containing trial data, called via RScript shell command
from within the database infrastructure (e.g. a PHP shell_exec call, with appropriate input sanitation).
It also assumes that the database infrasturcture allows use of the 
Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) API, but these code chunks
can be swapped out for whatever is relevant.

Data is read using the REDCap API, but the result is written to the database by passing
the treatment assignment to some other program that will handle write access. This
is a somewhat impractical approach in practice (i.e. in practice R would either
use an API for both read and write steps,or would not use the API at all).
It is used here for illustrative purposes only.

## Data import

```{r}

# If randomisation script is called from a command line call using Rscript,
# the ID can be passed as an argument

# args = commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
# id <- args[1]

id <- "5"

```


```{r}
# Use REDCap's API to load data

library(REDCapR)

# This token and URL are taken from the REDCapR vignettes and should be replaced
uri   <- "https://redcap-dev-2.ouhsc.edu/redcap/api/"
token <- "9A068C425B1341D69E83064A2D273A70"

read_data <- as.data.frame(redcap_read(redcap_uri = uri, token = token)$data)

```


```{r}
# In a trial data set, the arm would be one of the columns read from above
read_data$arm <- c(0,1,0,1,NA)

# Structure the data how we need it to be structured
# We use BMI and read_data as examples.
read_data <- read_data[,c("record_id","age","sex","bmi","ethnicity","arm")]
read_data$ethnicity <- factor(read_data$ethnicity, ordered=FALSE)
read_data$sex <- factor(read_data$sex, ordered=FALSE)


# The allocation function feeds in data separately for participants that have
# been randomised, and the participant to be randomised. We need to separate this out.

existing_data <- read_data[which(read_data$record_id != id),]
new_data <- read_data[which(read_data$record_id == id),]


```

Alternatively, data can be written to disk by some other mechanism and then read
by R using e.g. read.csv().

Regardless of the method of reading data, the final step prior to randomisation
is to perform checks of data quality. If randomisation requires data have to
complete data (all current methods need complete data), missing data in
existing data will break randomisation. The easiest fix for this is to simply allocate
imbalance based on complete case current data.

**NOTE** this workflow means that record deletion, or removal of a baseline covariate,
may lead to re-use of the random sequence. While in theory no record should be deleted
in practice and baseline covariate information should not be deleted, use the
optional offset argument in allocate() can be used to jump the sequence ahead
by a specified some number of allocations if this is needed.
The offset number will need to be calculated from the read data.

```{r}

# Run randomisation only using those people with complete data (i.e. treatment assigned and all relevant covariates observed)

has_missing <- do.call("c",
        sapply(1:ncol(existing_data),function(i){which(is.na(existing_data[,i]))})
)

if(length(has_missing)>0){
  existing_data[-has_missing,]
}

```

Also check for anything that looks wrong about the data, and error if we're missing
data on the new person.

```{r}

if(!is.na(new_data$arm)) stop(sprintf("ID %s is already randomised",id))

for(i in c("age","sex","bmi","ethnicity")){
  if(is.na(new_data[,i])) stop(sprintf("ID %s is missing a value for %s",id,i))
}

```


## Allocation

With data read and pre-processed, allocation can occur. 
The first step of allocation is to specify the design and randomisation sequence.
Ideally, this should be done ahead of time and stored on the machine as e.g. an RDS file.
This is especially important if the randomisation sequence is constrained
(e.g. permuted blocks), as it may take time to generate the sequence.


```{r}
randScheme <- csmsb(alpha = 0.4,biasParameters = 0.7)
randSequence <- get_randNumbers(500,n.trials = 1, trng = 1234)
```

Random allocation is then calculated using the package.

```{r}

new_assignment <- allocate(newData = new_data[,c("age","sex","bmi","ethnicity")], 
         data = existing_data[,c("age","sex","bmi","ethnicity")],
         arm = existing_data[,c("arm")],
         offset = 0,
         randomisationScheme =randScheme,
         randSequence = randSequence)

```

## Export

The final step is to write the result back into the database. This can be done
either via API call (following a similar structure as used earlier in the vignette to read data),
or by printing the results of randomisation to console, to be intercepted by another program.
This vignette illustrates the second approach.

If this code is called by an Rscript command line argument, then the infrastructure that
called the code will be able to capture whatever is output. Therefore, the simplest
way to communicate the results of randomisation back to trial database infrastructure
is to print the results of randomisation as a string which encodes the randomisation
as a JSON object. This JSON object can then be parsed by code within the trial database
infrastructure.

```{r}
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(new_assignment))
```
